references.text: Matthew's parallel account of Jesus' temptation in the wilderness, where the devil tempts Jesus three times and then leaves him.
Mark's concise account of Jesus' temptation in the wilderness, which parallels Luke's narrative.
The preceding verses in Luke that describe the actual temptations the devil completed (πάντα πειρασμόν) before withdrawing.
Jesus tells his disciples that they are those who have stood with him in his trials (πειρασμοῖς), linking back to the temptations he endured.
Satan enters Judas Iscariot – this marks the devil's return "until a more opportune time" (ἄχρι καιροῦ), as warned in Luke 4:13.
Jesus tells those who arrest him that "this is your hour and the power of darkness", indicating that the opportune time (καιρός) for the devil's attack has come.
Jesus says that "the ruler of this world is coming", referring to the devil's return after waiting for an opportune moment.
Because Christ himself suffered and was tempted, he can help those who are being tempted – this explains the significance of Jesus undergoing every temptation.
We have a high priest who has been tempted in every way just as we are, yet without sin – a theological reflection on how Jesus withstood all temptations (πάντα πειρασμόν).
"Resist the devil, and he will flee from you" – a principle illustrated by the devil fleeing from Jesus after he had resisted all temptations.
The devil prowls around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour – believers are urged to resist him, just as Jesus did in the wilderness.
